original_title: Xbox’s Disc-To-Digital Program Has A Big Problem: Several Major Publishers Aren’t Participating
summary_en: Xbox's initiative to let players digitize their old game discs faces a significant hurdle, with major publishers like Sega, Ubisoft, and Square Enix notably absent from the program.
ai_analysis: This situation highlights the ongoing tension between legacy physical media and the digital-first future, directly impacting how players can access and preserve their game libraries.

en.title: Xbox's Disc-To-Digital Program Stumbles as Key Publishers Opt Out
en.summary: Xbox's initiative to let players digitize their old game discs faces a significant hurdle, with major publishers like Sega, Ubisoft, and Square Enix notably absent from the program.
en.body:
Xbox's ambitious Disc-To-Digital program, designed to bridge the gap between physical game ownership and a digital future, is encountering a significant roadblock. While the service promises a convenient way for players to convert their old disc-based games into digital licenses on their Xbox accounts, a growing number of reports indicate that not all publishers are on board. This exclusion leaves a substantial portion of existing game collections incompatible with the program, frustrating fans who hoped to consolidate their libraries.

Several of the industry's biggest players, including **Sega**, **Square Enix**, **Ubisoft**, and **Bandai Namco**, are reportedly not participating in the Disc-To-Digital initiative. This means that physical copies of beloved titles from these publishers, such as **Final Fantasy XV**, **Dark Souls III**, or **Far Cry 4**, cannot be converted. When users attempt to digitize these games, they are met with messages indicating the titles are "not participating in digital licensing." This is a crucial limitation, as these publishers represent a vast catalog of games that many players still own physically.

## The Publisher's Perspective

The reasons behind this widespread non-participation likely stem from economic considerations and publisher control over their intellectual property. When a game is resold on the secondhand market, the original publisher typically sees no revenue from that transaction. By not allowing disc-to-digital conversions, publishers retain a stronger incentive for players to repurchase their games digitally on the Xbox Store, ensuring they receive revenue from every new acquisition. As seen with **Square Enix**'s approach to upgrades for their HD-2D RPGs on newer hardware, publishers are increasingly focused on direct digital sales and maximizing revenue streams. The decision ultimately rests with each publisher, as they own the rights to their games, and not all are willing to grant Xbox the necessary permissions for this conversion service.

## What This Means for Gamers

For dedicated Xbox fans, especially those who have cultivated extensive physical game libraries over the years, this news is a major disappointment. The Disc-To-Digital program was seen as a potential lifeline, allowing them to preserve access to games that might otherwise become unplayable due to aging disc drives or the eventual discontinuation of physical media. The exclusion of major publishers means that many cherished games will remain siloed in their physical form, inaccessible through the intended digital conversion. Community efforts to catalog which games *do* work with the service highlight just how many popular titles are currently left out, leaving fans to wonder if their collections will ever be fully digitized.

## What's Next

Xbox has indicated that the Disc-To-Digital program is a gradual rollout, suggesting that more publishers *could* eventually join. However, the current wording and the scale of the current non-participation suggest this may not be a swift or comprehensive solution. Players will need to keep an eye on official announcements from **Xbox** and individual publishers for any updates on future participation.

content_raw: Xbox's disc-to-digital program looks like it could be a vital step forward for players who want to hold on to their physical games in an increasingly digital world, but it does have limits. Not every game publisher is on board with it, it seems, as Xbox users are reporting that four of the biggest companies aren't "participating" at all. So far, it looks like games from Sega, Square Enix, Ubisoft, and Bandai Namco are largely incompatible with the disc-to-digital service. As verified by Kotaku , popping in a disc for a game from one of those publishers could result in a "not participating in digital licensing" message. A fan effort to catalogue all the games that do work with it also shows which titles from those publishers are incompatible with disc-to-digital, so if you were holding on to a physical edition of Far Cry 4, Final Fantasy 15, or Dark Souls 3, you're out of luck. This could be rectified in the future if those publishers decide to sign up--Xbox has mentioned that this will be a gradual rollout for the service--but the current wording of the message and the sheer number of games involved suggest otherwise. What's the reason for this? It could be down to good ol' economics, as the companies would probably prefer that you buy one of their games again on the digital storefront. After all, if you decide to pick up a physical copy of a title from a local secondhand store or through a private sale, they're not seeing a cent of that cash when it changes hands. This is something that Square Enix has been called to task over, as several of its big HD-2D RPGs have no upgrade path to Switch 2 . For example, if you purchased Octopath Traveler for the Switch, there's no complimentary or premium upgrade pack to give it sharper graphics and new features on a Switch 2 console. Instead, you'll have to buy the game again when its Switch 2 version launches, and you don't even get an option to transfer your save game over. All of this paints a worrying picture for game preservation, as Square Enix, Sega, Bandai Namco, and Ubisoft represent a sizable chunk of the gaming market with several big franchises and numerous smaller games spread between them. Microsoft may want to make the transition to an all-digital future easier --and better than Sony's plan to go all in on ditching physical media--but not every company wants to play ball.
